title: Design a payments API with idempotent charges
brief: Design the public API and backend for creating payments (charges) on behalf of merchants. Merchants call the API from their servers, often with retries on timeouts. A charge must never be executed twice, and the merchant must always be able to learn the final outcome, even when the downstream card network call times out.
constraints: 5k payment creations/s peak, 100M merchants' customers
p99 API latency < 500ms excluding the card network call
Card network/processor calls can take 1-10s and occasionally time out with unknown outcome
Zero tolerance for double charges; every state change must be auditable
Merchants retry aggressively on 5xx and network errors

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define what the API guarantees to merchants about retries, outcomes and consistency.
keyPoints: Create, retrieve, capture, cancel and refund a payment
Safe retries: the same request with the same Idempotency-Key yields the same result
Explicit payment state machine visible to merchants
Unknown outcomes from processors must be resolved, never guessed
Non-goals: fraud scoring and payouts (separate systems)

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Sketch the endpoints, idempotency semantics and error model.
keyPoints: POST /v1/payment_intents with Idempotency-Key header; amount in minor units + currency
GET /v1/payment_intents/{id}; POST .../confirm, .../capture, .../cancel; POST /v1/refunds
Same key + different params returns an error rather than a replay
Typed errors (card_error, invalid_request_error, api_error) with codes; 409 for a concurrent request with the same key
Date-based API versioning pinned per merchant account
Webhooks (payment_intent.succeeded etc.) for asynchronous outcomes

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model payments, attempts and idempotency records.
keyPoints: payments(id, merchant_id, amount, currency, status, version, created_at)
payment_attempts(id, payment_id, processor_ref, status, request/response) - one row per processor call
idempotency_keys(merchant_id, key, request_hash, status locked|done, response, expires_at) with unique (merchant_id, key)
Append-only event/audit log of every state transition
Ledger entries written by a separate ledger service from payment events

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Describe the request path for a create-and-confirm call.
keyPoints: API gateway: auth, rate limiting, versioning transforms
Idempotency layer: insert key row atomically (locked); if exists and done, replay stored response; if locked, 409
Payment service persists intent and attempt (status=pending) before calling the processor
Processor adapter with timeouts; result recorded, state machine advanced in a transaction
Outbox table to emit events to webhooks and ledger reliably
Store the final response under the idempotency key, including deterministic errors

sections.title: Scale & performance
sections.prompt: How do you scale to peak and keep latency down?
keyPoints: Shard payments and idempotency keys by merchant_id
Stateless API tier scaled horizontally
Idempotency key lookup is a primary-key read on the same shard as the payment
Async processing for slow methods (bank debits) with webhooks
Connection pooling and bulkheads per processor

sections.title: Failure modes & recovery
sections.prompt: Walk through timeouts and partial failures.
keyPoints: Processor timeout: mark attempt unknown, query processor status / reconcile later; never blind-retry a charge without processor-side idempotency
Pass our attempt id as the processor's idempotency reference
Crash after processor success but before DB commit: recovered by reconciliation against processor reports
Idempotency key stuck in locked state: lease with expiry and recovery job
Daily reconciliation of payments vs processor settlement files vs ledger

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Discuss alternatives and their costs.
keyPoints: Synchronous confirm (simple for merchants) vs async (resilient to slow rails)
Storing full responses for replay costs storage but guarantees identical retries
Strong consistency per merchant shard vs global consistency
Key TTL (e.g. 24h) bounds storage but limits how late retries are safe
Client-generated keys put responsibility on merchants; SDKs generate them automatically

modelSummary: Accept payments through a resource-oriented API where every mutating request carries an idempotency key stored atomically with a request fingerprint and final response. Persist intent and attempt before calling the processor, pass attempt ids as processor idempotency references, and model payments as an explicit state machine. Unknown outcomes are resolved by status queries and reconciliation, events leave via an outbox to webhooks and the ledger, and data is sharded by merchant.

title: Design a webhook delivery system
brief: Merchants register HTTPS endpoints to receive events (payment succeeded, dispute created, ...). Design the system that delivers every event to every subscribed endpoint reliably, securely and without letting slow or broken merchant endpoints hurt everyone else.
constraints: 20k events/s generated, average fan-out 1.5 endpoints
Merchant endpoints have wildly varying latency; many are down at any time
At-least-once delivery; retries for up to ~3 days
Payloads must be verifiable as coming from us
Merchants want to see delivery history and replay events

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Pin down delivery guarantees and merchant-facing features.
keyPoints: At-least-once delivery per (event, endpoint); no ordering guarantee, documented
Retries with exponential backoff over days; then mark failed and alert merchant
Signed payloads with timestamp to prevent spoofing and replay
Dashboard: delivery attempts, response codes, manual resend
Endpoint subscribes to selected event types

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define the merchant-facing configuration API and payload contract.
keyPoints: POST /v1/webhook_endpoints {url, enabled_events}; returns a signing secret
Event payload: {id, type, created, api_version, data.object}
Header with timestamp and HMAC-SHA256 signature over timestamp.payload; support secret rotation with multiple signatures
GET /v1/events and resend endpoint for recovery
Receivers must return 2xx quickly and dedupe on event id

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: What do you store?
keyPoints: events(id, account_id, type, payload, created) - immutable
endpoints(id, account_id, url, secret, events, status)
deliveries(event_id, endpoint_id, attempt, next_attempt_at, status, last_response_code)
Index on next_attempt_at for the scheduler
Retention policy on events (e.g. 30 days)

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Describe the pipeline from event creation to HTTP POST.
keyPoints: Producers write events via outbox to a durable log (e.g. Kafka) partitioned by account
Fan-out service resolves subscribed endpoints and creates delivery tasks
Delivery workers make HTTP calls with short timeouts, sign payloads, record results
Failed deliveries go to a delay scheduler (timer wheel / delay queues per backoff tier)
Per-endpoint concurrency limits and circuit breakers
Egress through fixed IP proxies; SSRF protection blocking internal addresses

sections.title: Scale & performance
sections.prompt: How do you handle volume and noisy endpoints?
keyPoints: Partition work by endpoint so slow endpoints don't block others
Separate queues for healthy vs struggling endpoints
Adaptive concurrency per endpoint based on latency/error rate
Batch DB writes of delivery attempts
Horizontal worker scaling on queue lag

sections.title: Failure modes & recovery
sections.prompt: What goes wrong and how do you recover?
keyPoints: Endpoint down for days: backoff with jitter, then disable endpoint and email merchant
Worker crash mid-delivery: task re-leased, causing a duplicate - acceptable under at-least-once
Mass outage on our side: backlog drains with rate limits to avoid thundering herd
Merchant secret leaked: rotation with overlapping secrets
Malicious URL targets internal network: SSRF filtering and DNS rebinding checks

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare design options.
keyPoints: At-least-once + idempotent receivers vs exactly-once (impossible across an HTTP boundary)
Ordering per object would require serial delivery and head-of-line blocking; instead include timestamps and let merchants fetch latest state
Push webhooks vs pull (events API): offer both
Thin events (ids only) vs full payloads: thin avoids stale data but costs an extra API call
DB-backed scheduler is simpler; dedicated delay queue scales better

modelSummary: Events are written once via an outbox to a durable log, fanned out into per-endpoint delivery tasks, and delivered by workers that sign payloads (HMAC over timestamp and body) and enforce short timeouts. Failures are rescheduled with exponential backoff and jitter for days, isolated per endpoint with concurrency limits and circuit breakers. Delivery is at-least-once with no ordering guarantee, so receivers dedupe on event id; an events API and resend tooling cover recovery.

title: Design a double-entry ledger
brief: Design the internal ledger that records every movement of money across Stripe-like balances: customer charges, fees, refunds, disputes and payouts to merchants. Finance and other services must be able to trust balances, reconstruct history at any point in time and reconcile against banks.
constraints: Billions of entries per year; 50k entries/s peak
Balances must be correct and never silently drift
Immutable history; corrections are new entries
Multi-currency
Read balance for a merchant in < 50ms

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: What must the ledger guarantee?
keyPoints: Every transaction is a set of entries summing to zero per currency
Append-only and immutable, with point-in-time balance queries
Idempotent posting from upstream services
Reconciliation with external bank and processor statements
Auditability: link each entry to its source event

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define posting and query interfaces.
keyPoints: postTransaction(idempotency_key, entries[{account, amount, currency, direction}], metadata)
Reject if entries don't balance per currency
getBalance(account, currency, as_of?)
listEntries(account, from, to, cursor)
Async event stream of posted transactions for downstream consumers

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model accounts, transactions and entries.
keyPoints: accounts(id, owner, type: asset/liability/revenue/expense, currency)
transactions(id, idempotency_key unique, source_ref, posted_at)
entries(id, transaction_id, account_id, amount signed minor units, currency)
balance snapshots(account, currency, as_of_seq, balance) for fast reads
Sequence number per account for ordering and optimistic concurrency

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: How are postings written and balances served?
keyPoints: Ledger service validates balance-to-zero and writes transaction + entries atomically
Partition by account; cross-partition transactions via a single-writer per transaction log or 2-phase posting
Balance = latest snapshot + entries since snapshot; or maintained running balance updated in same transaction
Consumers of upstream events (payments, refunds) translate into postings using rule tables
Reconciliation jobs compare ledger to bank/processor files and flag breaks

sections.title: Scale & performance
sections.prompt: How do you scale writes and hot accounts?
keyPoints: Hot accounts (e.g. Stripe's fee revenue) get sharded sub-accounts summed on read
Batch postings for high-volume flows
Log-structured design: write to an ordered log, materialise balances asynchronously
Archive old entries to cold storage with snapshots
Read replicas for history queries

sections.title: Failure modes & recovery
sections.prompt: How do you detect and fix errors?
keyPoints: Continuous invariant checks: sum of all entries per currency = 0
Upstream duplicate events are absorbed by idempotency keys
Wrong posting: fix with reversing entries, never update/delete
Reconciliation breaks trigger alerts and manual investigation workflows
Replay ability: rebuild balances from the entry log

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Discuss design alternatives.
keyPoints: Running balances (fast reads, write contention) vs computed on read (slow) vs snapshots (hybrid)
Strict synchronous balance checks vs eventual consistency for non-overdraft accounts
Relational DB with transactions vs event log + materialised views
Single global ledger vs per-domain ledgers aggregated
Granularity of accounts: per merchant per currency per balance type

modelSummary: An append-only, double-entry ledger where each idempotent transaction consists of entries that sum to zero per currency. Entries are immutable; corrections are reversing entries. Balances are served from snapshots plus recent entries (or running balances), hot accounts are split into sub-accounts, and continuous invariant checks plus reconciliation against external statements detect drift.

title: Design a rate limiter for an API platform
brief: Design rate limiting and load shedding for a public API used by millions of businesses. It must protect the platform from abusive or buggy clients and from overload, while ensuring critical traffic (like payment creation) keeps working during incidents.
constraints: ~100k requests/s across a global fleet
Per-account limits (e.g. 100 req/s in live mode, lower in test mode)
p99 overhead < 2ms
Critical endpoints must be prioritised during overload
Limiter failures must not take down the API

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: What kinds of limits and shedding are needed?
keyPoints: Per-account request rate limiter (token bucket)
Concurrency limiter for expensive endpoints
Fleet-level load shedder that sheds low-priority traffic first
Clear 429 responses with retry guidance
Fail open if the limiter store is unavailable

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: How do limits surface to callers and operators?
keyPoints: 429 Too Many Requests with error code rate_limit and Retry-After
Internal check(account, endpoint, cost) -> allow/deny + remaining
Admin config: per-account overrides and per-endpoint costs
Client SDKs retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Metrics per account for support and dashboards

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: What state do you keep?
keyPoints: Token bucket per (account, limit) in Redis: tokens + last refill
Concurrency counters with TTL leases
Config cached locally in gateways
Priority classification table for endpoints
Counters for observability

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Where does enforcement happen?
keyPoints: Middleware in API gateway calls Redis with atomic Lua script
Local in-memory pre-check to shed obvious abuse
Load shedder uses fleet utilisation signals to drop non-critical traffic (e.g. reads/test mode) before critical
Redis cluster sharded by account key
Dark-launch new limits and observe before enforcing

sections.title: Scale & performance
sections.prompt: How do you keep latency and store load low?
keyPoints: Single round trip per check via Lua script
Local token leasing for very high-volume accounts
Shard keys across Redis nodes; replicas for failover
Avoid hot keys by splitting very large accounts' buckets
Pipeline multiple limit checks per request

sections.title: Failure modes & recovery
sections.prompt: What happens when parts fail?
keyPoints: Redis down: fail open with local approximate limits
Retry storms after incidents: jittered backoff in SDKs
Misconfigured limit: dark launch, gradual rollout, quick override
Clock skew: compute refill in Redis using server time
Overload: shed by priority instead of uniformly

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Compare approaches.
keyPoints: Token bucket (bursty, cheap) vs sliding window (smoother, more state)
Centralised store (accurate) vs local (fast, approximate)
Fail open (availability) vs fail closed (protection)
Request rate vs concurrency limits - both needed for slow endpoints
Uniform shedding vs priority shedding

modelSummary: Layered protection: per-account token buckets in a sharded Redis via atomic scripts, concurrency limiters for expensive endpoints, and a fleet-level load shedder that drops low-priority traffic first so payment creation survives incidents. Limits return 429 with retry guidance, SDKs back off with jitter, the limiter fails open, and new limits are dark-launched before enforcement.

title: Design a subscription billing engine
brief: Design a system that lets merchants define plans and bill customers on recurring schedules: monthly/annual cycles, trials, upgrades and downgrades with proration, usage-based components, invoices, and automatic retries of failed payments (dunning).
constraints: 50M active subscriptions; many renew at midnight UTC on the 1st
Invoices must be correct to the minor unit and reproducible
Plan changes mid-cycle with proration
Usage events: 200k/s ingested
Merchants in many time zones and currencies

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define the scope of billing.
keyPoints: Plans/prices with interval, currency, flat or per-unit or tiered
Subscription lifecycle: trialing, active, past_due, canceled
Proration on plan changes; billing anchors
Invoice generation, finalisation, payment and dunning retries
Usage-based billing with aggregation per period

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Sketch the key resources and calls.
keyPoints: POST /v1/subscriptions {customer, items[price, quantity], trial_end}
POST /v1/subscriptions/{id} to change items with proration_behavior
POST /v1/usage_records (idempotent) for metered prices
Invoices: draft -> open -> paid/uncollectible/void
Webhooks: invoice.created, invoice.payment_failed, customer.subscription.updated

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model the core entities.
keyPoints: products, prices(amount, currency, interval, tiers)
subscriptions(id, customer, status, current_period_start/end, anchor)
subscription_items(price, quantity)
invoices + invoice_line_items (including proration lines), immutable once finalised
usage aggregates per (subscription_item, period)

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: How does renewal and invoicing run?
keyPoints: Scheduler indexes subscriptions by next_billing_at; workers claim due ones with leases
Invoice builder computes lines deterministically from subscription state at period boundary
Draft period (e.g. ~1h) allows merchant edits before finalisation
Payment via payments API with idempotency key derived from invoice id
Dunning service retries failed payments on a schedule, updates status

sections.title: Scale & performance
sections.prompt: How do you deal with the midnight-on-the-1st spike?
keyPoints: Spread work: pre-compute drafts ahead of time, process within window
Partition scheduler by subscription id hash
Rate-limit payment attempts per processor
Usage ingestion via stream with pre-aggregation
Backpressure without missing billing deadlines

sections.title: Failure modes & recovery
sections.prompt: What can go wrong?
keyPoints: Worker crash mid-invoice: idempotent invoice creation per (subscription, period)
Double billing prevented via unique constraint on period
Late usage events: cutoff policy, add to next invoice
Payment failure: dunning, then cancel or mark unpaid per merchant settings
Bug in proration: invoices are immutable; issue credit notes

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Discuss alternatives.
keyPoints: Batch nightly billing vs continuous scheduler
Proration exactness (to the second) vs simplicity (by day)
Real-time usage totals vs periodic aggregation
Merchant-specific time zones vs UTC anchors
Rounding: round per line vs per invoice - define and document

modelSummary: Subscriptions reference prices and are renewed by a partitioned scheduler that claims due subscriptions with leases and builds invoices deterministically per (subscription, period), guarded by uniqueness constraints. Proration produces explicit line items, invoices become immutable on finalisation with credit notes for corrections, payments use idempotency keys derived from invoice ids, and dunning retries failures. Usage is ingested via a stream and pre-aggregated per period.

title: Design a fraud-check and payout pipeline
brief: Design the pipeline that (a) scores every payment for fraud risk inline before authorisation and (b) pays out merchants' available balances to their bank accounts on a schedule, holding funds when risk is detected.
constraints: Inline fraud decision budget: < 100ms p99
10k payments/s peak
Daily payouts to millions of merchant bank accounts via batch bank rails
False positives cost merchants revenue; false negatives cost money
Payouts must never be sent twice

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define scoring and payout scope.
keyPoints: Real-time risk score per payment with allow / review / block decisions
Merchant-configurable rules on top of ML scores
Payouts: compute available balance, create payout, submit to bank, track status
Holds and reserves for risky merchants
Audit trail for every decision

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: What interfaces exist?
keyPoints: Internal score(payment features) -> {score, decision, reasons}
Rules API for merchants (e.g. block if CVC fails)
POST /v1/payouts (manual) and automatic schedule settings
Payout statuses: pending, in_transit, paid, failed, canceled
Webhooks: payout.paid, payout.failed, review.opened

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: What data supports both?
keyPoints: Feature store: velocity counters (card, IP, device, email) with low-latency reads
Decisions log with model version and features
Balances from the ledger (available vs pending)
payouts(id, merchant, amount, currency, status, bank_ref, idempotency key)
Bank files submitted and returned

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Describe both paths.
keyPoints: Inline: payment service -> scoring service (features + model + rules) with strict timeout and fallback decision
Async: events stream updates velocity features and trains models offline
Payout scheduler reads available balance from ledger, reserves funds by posting ledger entries, creates payout
Bank adapter batches payouts into rail-specific files/API calls, tracks acknowledgements
Return/failure files reverse ledger entries and notify merchant

sections.title: Scale & performance
sections.prompt: How do you meet latency and volume?
keyPoints: Precomputed features in an in-memory store; model served in-process
Shadow-mode new models before enforcing
Payouts partitioned by merchant and rail cut-off times
Batching per bank rail
Backfills and replays of feature pipelines

sections.title: Failure modes & recovery
sections.prompt: What fails and how do you recover?
keyPoints: Scoring timeout: fall back to rules-only or default allow under threshold
Feature store stale: degrade gracefully, alert
Duplicate payout risk: unique payout per (merchant, schedule date) and bank-side reference dedupe
Bank returns funds days later: reverse ledger, mark failed, re-attempt after bank details fix
Model drift: monitor approval and dispute rates

sections.title: Trade-offs & alternatives
sections.prompt: Discuss trade-offs.
keyPoints: Fail-open vs fail-closed on scoring outage (revenue vs loss)
Inline ML (precision) vs simple rules (latency, explainability)
Rolling reserves vs delayed payouts for risky merchants
Instant payouts (cost, risk) vs batch
Per-merchant thresholds vs global model

modelSummary: Inline fraud scoring combines low-latency precomputed velocity features, an in-process model and merchant rules under a strict timeout with a defined fallback, logging every decision. Payouts are driven by a scheduler that reads available balance from the ledger, reserves funds with ledger entries, creates uniquely keyed payouts and submits them in batches per bank rail; bank returns reverse the entries. Holds and reserves connect risk to payouts.
